facts: $y=\arcsin x$ is the reflection of $y=\sin x$, restricted to $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{\pi}{2}$, in the line $y=x$.
$y=\arcsin x$ has domain $-1\le x\le1$ and range $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le y\le\frac{\pi}{2}$, increasing from $\left(-1,-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ to $\left(1,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
$y=\arccos x$ is the reflection of $y=\cos x$, restricted to $0\le x\le\pi$, in the line $y=x$.
$y=\arccos x$ has domain $-1\le x\le1$ and range $0\le y\le\pi$, decreasing from $(-1,\pi)$ to $(1,0)$.
$y=\arctan x$ is the reflection of $y=\tan x$, restricted to $-\frac{\pi}{2}<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$, in the line $y=x$.
$y=\arctan x$ has domain all real $x$ and range $-\frac{\pi}{2}<y<\frac{\pi}{2}$.
The vertical asymptotes $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$ of the restricted $y=\tan x$ become the horizontal asymptotes $y=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$ of $y=\arctan x$.
$y=\arcsin x$ and $y=\arccos x$ stop at endpoints where $x=\pm1$, so neither of them has an asymptote.
steps: Sketch the restricted trigonometric graph over its principal domain.
Reflect the restricted graph in the line $y=x$ by swapping the coordinates of the key points.
Swap the domain and the range, turning any vertical asymptote into a horizontal asymptote.
Sketch the inverse curve through the reflected key points and state its domain and range.

foundation.solution_text:
Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps the domain and the range of the restricted graph.
Restricted $y=\sin x$ has domain $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{\pi}{2}$ and range $-1\le y\le1$.
Domain of $y=\arcsin x$: $-1\le x\le1$
Range of $y=\arcsin x$: $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le y\le\frac{\pi}{2}$

Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps the domain and the range of the restricted graph.
Restricted $y=\cos x$ has domain $0\le x\le\pi$ and range $-1\le y\le1$.
Domain of $y=\arccos x$: $-1\le x\le1$
Range of $y=\arccos x$: $0\le y\le\pi$

Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps the coordinates of the point.
$\left(\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{1}{2}\right)\to\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$

Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps the coordinates of the point.
$\left(\frac{2\pi}{3},-\frac{1}{2}\right)\to\left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$

Reflecting in $y=x$ turns a vertical asymptote $x=k$ into a horizontal asymptote $y=k$.
$x=\frac{\pi}{2}\to y=\frac{\pi}{2}$
$x=-\frac{\pi}{2}\to y=-\frac{\pi}{2}$

The curve has domain $-1\le x\le1$ and range $0\le y\le\pi$, and it decreases from $(-1,\pi)$ to $(1,0)$.
Only the reflection of $y=\cos x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$ has these features.
$y=\arccos x$

development.solution_text:
Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps the coordinates, so a vertical line $x=k$ becomes the horizontal line $y=k$.
The asymptotes $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$ therefore become the horizontal asymptotes $y=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.
The restricted $y=\tan x$ is undefined at $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$, so $\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$ is not in the range of $y=\arctan x$ and the curve never reaches those lines.

Both restricted graphs have range $-1\le y\le1$, and reflecting in $y=x$ makes that the domain.
Common domain: $-1\le x\le1$
Range of $y=\arcsin x$: $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le y\le\frac{\pi}{2}$
Range of $y=\arccos x$: $0\le y\le\pi$

Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps the coordinates of the point.
$\left(\frac{\pi}{4},1\right)\to\left(1,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$
The point $\left(1,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ lies on $y=\arctan x$, so $\arctan 1=\frac{\pi}{4}$.

The curve is defined for every real $x$, so it cannot be $y=\arcsin x$ or $y=\arccos x$.
It increases through the origin between the horizontal asymptotes $y=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.
$y=\arctan x$

mastery.solution_text:
The line $y=\frac{1}{2}$ cuts the curve twice, at $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$ and at $x=\frac{5\pi}{3}$.
So the value $\frac{1}{2}$ comes from two different inputs, and $y=\cos x$ is not one-to-one on $0\le x\le2\pi$.
Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps those two points to $\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$ and $\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)$, which share an $x$-value, so the reflection fails the vertical line test.
Restricting the domain to $0\le x\le\pi$ makes $y=\cos x$ one-to-one, and the reflection is then the function $y=\arccos x$.

A point $(k,b)$ on $y=\arccos x$ comes from the point $(b,k)$ on the restricted $y=\cos x$.
So $k=\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}$
$=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$
The corresponding point on the restricted $y=\cos x$ is $\left(\frac{3\pi}{4},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$.
